title: A three-in-one strategy for lithium recovery and upcycling of spent cathode materials

paper_content.introduction:
The rapid application of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) as essential cleanenergystoragedevicesinelectricvehicles,portableelectronics,andgrid-scalestorageisgeneratingagrowingstreamofspentbatteries1,2.TheglobalvolumeofspentLIBsisprojectedtoreach381millionmetrictonsby20503.Impropermanagementofsuchwastestreamsmaynotonlyresultinsubstantialwasteofstrategicmetalresourcessuchaslithium(Li)4,cobalt(Co),andnickel(Ni)butalso pose major environmental pollution risks, which threaten ecosystems and human health. Consequently, the efficient recovery of critical metals from spent LIBs is crucial for economic, environmental,andsocialsustainability5,6.

Current recycling of critical metals from spent LIBs relies on threeprincipalroutes:pyrometallurgy,hydrometallurgy,anddirectregeneration7. Pyrometallurgy uses high-temperature smelting (typically >1400°C)8torecoverCo, NiandCu,whiletherecoveryratesoflithiumaswellasFeandP(inaLiFePO4battery)arelow.Theprocessisinherentwithstringentrequirementsforinputmaterials andhighenergyconsumption6.Incontrast,hydrometallurgyoffers improved recovery efficiency for different elements through chemicalleachingwithsolventssuchasmineral/organicacidsordeep eutecticsolvents9–11.Nevertheless,conventionalhydrometallurgical processes often encounter challenges, such as high chemical consumption and lengthy purification sequences12. Direct regenerationisapromisingalternativethatemploysshorterprocessingroutestorestoredegradedcathodematerials(e.g.,viasolid-state, sol-gel, or hydrothermal Li replenishment)13–15 or increases cell capacity(e.g.,usingLi-compensatingadditivessuchasLi-Naph)16,17. However, its practical application is limited because it can only process less complex spent LIB streams18. Comparative analysis identifieshydrometallurgyasthemostversatileandwidelyapplicable approach, combining moderate energy requirements, adaptabilitytodiversebatterychemistries,andtuneablemetalseparationprocesses.

Compared with impurity-sensitive conventional hydrometallurgy, selective leaching improves Li recovery and simplifies purification19,20. The mechanisms preferentially induce targeted phasetransformationsinspentcathodes,separatingLifromtransitionmetal(TM)phases,drivenbystrategiessuchasaddingreductants or applying elevated temperature/pressure21. For example, carbothermic reduction converts spent cathodes into lithium carbonate(Li2CO3)andTMelementsortheiroxides20,22,23,andsulfationroastingyieldslithiumsulfate(Li2SO4)andTMoxides24–26.However, these methods often require substantial reagent inputs, produce hazardousemissionsandsecondarypollution,andgenerateleachingresidues.Theseresiduesusuallyrequireacidleachingforconversioninto salt solutions prior to reuse, which severely decreases their value. Consequently, optimizing resource utilization across the selective leaching chain requiresgreener, more efficient processes andsolutionsformanaginglow-valueresidues.FlashJouleheating27 can enable one-step selective Li extraction via second-long, high-temperature reactions. This instantaneous heating offers greener processinganduniquelyinducesstructuraltransformationsinspentcathodes, which could convert residual metals into self-assembled multi-metal hydroxide catalysts28. Electrochemical methods selectivelyleachLiatambienttemperaturebyusinganappliedpotential. The resulting structurally defective, Li-depleted residue can serve directlyasafunctionalmaterial,suchasanoxygenevolutionreaction(OER)catalyst,butelectrodereconstructionrequirementshinder scale-up29–31. Mechanical methods selectively leach Li through induced room-temperature phase transitions32; however, grinding additivesareassociatedwiththeriskofimpuritycontamination33,34.

Insummary,existingtechnologieshaveyettooptimallybalancemild processingconditions,minimalchemicalinput,andtheproduction ofhigh-valueoutputs.

Here,weproposea“Three-in-One”strategythatleverageselemental micro-segregation in spent cathode materials, which is inducedthroughcontrolledmechanochemical(MC)treatment.ThisinnovativeapproachenablesthesimultaneousselectiveextractionofLiandthetransformationofTM-basedleachingproductsintoOERcatalystsusingonlyCO2,asdepictedinFig.1a.Theentireprocedurewasconductedatambienttemperaturewithouttheuseofgrindingaidsorleachingagents.Notably,CO2fixationoccurssimultaneouslyduringthemetalrecoveryprocess.OurstrategyisinspiredbypriorworkonthesynthesisofLi-richdisorderedrocksaltcathodematerials (DRX)35, which showed that ball-milling could alter the initial distributionofLiandTMelementswithinthecathode,creatingLi-rich domains and increasing the charge–discharge capacity. The mechanical forceinourstudyservesasimilarpurposeofdisorderingthearrangementofLiandTMelementstoinducetheirmicro-segregation,whichendowstheseelementswithvaryingleachingactivities.Ultimately, this micro-segregation results in a Li leaching efficiency of >95% only with CO2—which could be prospectively derived entirely from industrial waste streams—thereby enhancing theenvironmentalandeconomicbenefitsoftheprocess.Moreover, thesynergisticeffectsofMCtreatmentandselectiveLiextractionin aweaklyacidicenvironmentresultinthecreationofacatalystwith exceptionalOERperformance.

After leaching, the final lixivium was separated from the leaching product(MA-LTMO-CO2L)through filtration. reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript presents a short-range clean recycling approach for spent lithium-ion battery cathodes, convincingly demonstrating the efficiency of mechanochemical processes through robust evidence. The mechnochemical treatment enables recycling of spent NCM battery under relatively mild conditions. With carbonation of the as-treated black mass, lithium and transition metals recovery are both achieved. Nevertheless, there are still issues required to be discussed before publication.
In extracting valuable metals from spent cathode materials, CO2 as leaching reagent is usually considered as inefficient. The authors should provide detailed discussion on how the mechnochemical treatment enables a high reaction potential. Will the amorphous phase be important during the processing? How was the optimal activation time was determined?
- Improvement on discussion of state-of-the-art of literature is very necessary and how selective leaching and upcycling of cathode materials are explored should be added in the introduction section.
- The authors mentioned “Notably, prolonged activation time (activation time >2 h) leads to gradual dissolution of TMs”. What are gradual dissolution and how the dissolution the transition metals reacting with CO2? It is necessary to provide direct evidence on the intermediate products. Additionally, a thermodynamic analysis will be helpful for understanding the process.
- The research object of the manuscript focuses on ternary materials. Is LCO with a layered structure also feasible? Is LiFePO4 or LiMn2O4 also feasible? Can some experiments or explanations be added to improve the universality of the raw materials?
- The authors detected oxygen vacancies in the leaching residue, while at which stage the oxygen vacancies appeared is required to be clarified. For example, do oxygen vacancies exist in the mechanically activated products? Or do oxygen vacancies exist in the waste materials used in this study? Additional results is recommended to improve understanding the mechanisms.
- In Figure 3, the authors claims “a Li-rich surface reconstruction layer have been established on the surface of materials.” However, it is not clear how the layer is defined. Will the surface be easily peeling off if a reconstructed layer is formed?
- Error bars for the leaching efficiencies in the corresponding figures are required to be added to reflect the repeatability and statistical validity of the data.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this work, the authors proposed a three-in-one strategy that enables CO2-carbonation with spent cathode materials to achieve selective Li recovery and regeneration of transition metals. The study conducts an in-depth analysis of how mechnochemical (MC) treatment affects the reactivity of different elements in cathode materials and the underlying mechanisms, providing new insights on the role of MC treatment in the recycling process. I think it can be considered for publication if the following concerns are tackled with.
(1)The introduction can be enriched and a more detailed discussion on selective leaching and direct regeneration is required to be included. The authors only mentioned briefly the pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgical methods at this version and the statement on “...process requires a large amount of strong acid and alkali...” is not always correct. It is necessary to provide an outline on how this research is correlated and different from a traditional hydrometallurgical process.
(2)In addition to destroying the crystal structure, the MC process will also reduce the particle size. Together with the size reduction, how it is related to the leaching process, including lithium and other elements?
(3)A detailed description on how the amorphous content in Figure 1 was determined should be provided. How is the amorphous phase influencing the subsequent recycling process?
(4)What is the phase of the residual Li in the leaching product? It is required to discuss the carbonation process and how CO2 pressure and leaching time influence the lithium extraction.
(5)On page 10, the author present the Raman spectrum data of P-NCM811 and MA-NCM811 in Figure 4c. However, this section is unclearly articulated and lacks a robust connection to the contextual discussion. It is advised to revise this part for better coherence.
(6)Some details in Figures still need to be noted. In Figure 4e, the scale of TEM results is missing; in Figure 5e, the unit of the y-axis should be revised to mA cm-2.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The following are reviewer comments for the article entitled A Three-in-One Strategy: Li/TMs Micro-Segregation to Enable Upcycling of Spent Layered Cathode Materials submitted to Nature Communications by Wang et al.
The reviewed article has successfully demonstrated the novel approach of the selective Li recovery from spent Li-ion cathodes and upgrading of transition metals during mechanochemical processes assisted by CO2 sequestration. The Authors performed the broad compositional and structural products analysis and OER catalytic activity. I recommend publishing the article after a major review, and below are the comments and remarks:
1. Could the Authors describe the XRD results shown in Figure 1b by ascribing the peaks to the proper compounds?
2. What purity do the recovered Li compounds exhibit?
3. How does the morphology (e.g., grain size, grain shape) of examined materials change upon mechanochemical processing? Whether SEM analysis was done before and after the MC process?
4. Were OER experiments performed also for benchmark OER materials e.g. RuO2 or Co3O4 for comparison with recovered catalyst materials?
5. At which potential were the chronoamperometry measurements performed shown in Fig. 5e?
6. 6. The description of the Y axis should be “current density” instead of “current”.
7. The Electrochemical Active Surface Area should be ascertained in order to assess the OER catalytic capabilities.

Reviewer #1:
The manuscript presents a short-range clean recycling approach for spent lithium-ion
battery cathodes, convincingly demonstrating the efficiency of mechanochemical
processes through robust evidence. The mechanochemical treatment enables recycling
of spent NCM battery under relatively mild conditions. With carbonation of the as-
treated black mass, lithium and transition metals recovery are both achieved.
Nevertheless, there are still issues required to be discussed before publication.
Issue 1:
In extracting valuable metals from spent cathode materials, CO as leaching reagent is
2
usually considered as inefficient. The authors should provide detailed discussion on
how the mechanochemical treatment enables a high reaction potential. Will the
amorphous phase be important during the processing? How was the optimal activation
time was determined?
Discussion:
Thank you for your constructive comment and thoughtful questions.
Generally, CO is considered a relatively inefficient leaching agent for extracting
2
valuable metals from spent cathode materials, which is why it is not typically used as
the primary reagent. The mechanochemical (MC) process proposed in this study,
however, fundamentally alters the physicochemical properties of the original LTMO
cathode material. By creating a highly amorphous, defect-rich structure with a large
specific surface area, the MC treatment transforms the lattice Li into a state that is
highly reactive toward both H O and CO , thereby overcoming the inherent limitation
2 2
of directly leaching pristine cathodes with CO . We supplemented the detailed
2
discussion on how the mechanochemical treatment enables a high reaction potential in
Section 2.4 of the revised manuscript, as detailed below.
The resulting high degree of amorphization in MC process is the key to the success
of this process. This amorphization transforms the LTMO from the original stable and
ordered R-3m lattice structure into a composite consisting of a Li-rich amorphous phase
and a crystalline phase that is highly disordered and enriched with TMs. Analysis of the
leaching behavior of various elements in both aqueous and CO systems, as well as the
2
phase composition changes before and after leaching, indicates that the Li within the
amorphous phase exhibits water-soluble characteristics. For example, activated
NCM811 achieves approximately 75% Li leaching efficiency in aqueous system. The
presence of this soluble Li contributes significantly to the highly efficient Li extraction
enabled in CO system.
evidence, concluding structural evolution of LTMO and leaching performance of Li and
TMs. First, the XRD patterns in Figure R1 show that the degree of amorphization of
NCM811 increases markedly with activation time. After 2 h, the activated product
contains the highest fraction of amorphous phase and the most disordered residual
crystalline components. Second, the leaching results in Figure R2 indicate that the
activated product with activation time of 2h achieves a Li extraction yield of 75 % in
aqueous system, with no further significant improvement upon prolonged activation.
The effect is even more pronounced in the acidic system, 2 h of MC process gives the
highest Li leaching efficiency and selectivity, whereas longer activation times only
marginally increase Li recovery while substantially enhancing TMs dissolution. These
findings suggest that excessive activation triggers detrimental side reactions and
reduces Li selectivity. Therefore, 2 h is chosen as the optimal activation time, balancing
maximum structural disorder with the best Li recovery while avoiding the loss of
selectivity. Although this optimal condition was established for NCM811, it also proves
effective for other layered ternary cathodes such as NCM111 and NCM622.
Nonetheless, given the distinct structural characteristics of low-nickel ternary cathode
materials, further optimization of activation parameters is warranted and will be
explored in future work.

Thank you very much for your insightful questions.
Regarding the mechanism of “gradual dissolution” of TM in the acidic system,
this study specifies that the phenomenon refers to the dynamic process whereby TM2+
migrate from the mechanochemically activated crystal structure into the acidic solution
phase and remain stable. As shown in Section 2.1, the leaching efficiencies of TMs
from MA-NCM811 initially decreases and then increases with prolonged activation
time, which stems from the modulating effect of mechanical activation duration on the
crystal structure. At the optimal activation time of 2 h, Li+ is sufficiently released while
TM ions remain well retained within a relatively intact lattice framework. And further
extending the activation time, TMs started to migrate into the solution. As for the reason
of TMs dissolution, we monitored the final pH in both aqueous and acidic systems
(Figure R3a) revealed no significant change in the aqueous system, indicating that
water-soluble Li+ reached saturation at 2 h. In contrast, the pH in the acidic system first
increased and then decreased, accompanied by a slight reduction in Li leaching
efficiency and an increase in TM leaching efficiencies, confirming that the leaching
pathways of Li and TMs evolve with mechanical energy input. Ultimately, excessive
activation time diminished the difference in leaching activity between Li and TM,
maintaining the solution pH within a range that allows dissolution of low-valence TM
(e.g., Ni2+). We added the E-pH diagram (Figures R3b-d) obtained from HSC
Chemistry, validating that when the pH is lower than 7, Ni2+ exist primarily as ionic
species in the solution within Ni-H O system. Furthermore, characterization results
2
confirmed the reduction of Ni3+ to Ni2+ (Figure R4), providing a key prerequisite for
TM dissolution.

2

2 2 2 3

3 3

diagram in the TM-CO -H O system as shown in Figure R5a-c, low-valence TM ions
2 2

infrared (FTIR) spectrum of the leaching product (Figure R5d).
The activation process results in the divergent reaction pathways and the
intermediate products of TMs in the acidic and CO systems, and related

Issue 4:
The research object of the manuscript focuses on ternary materials. Is LCO with a
layered structure also feasible? Is LiFePO4 or LiMn2O4 also feasible? Can some
experiments or explanations be added to improve the universality of the raw materials?
Discussion:
Thank you for your practical questions. This study initially focused primarily on
ternary materials with a layered structure. Owing to their unique structural
characteristics and Ni-containing content, the effect of mechanical energy is more
pronounced. However, we did neglect to investigate the impact of the MC process on
LiCoO (LCO) also with a layered structure, and other common non-layered cathode
2
materials. In response to your inquiry, we have supplemented the data on the leaching
efficiency of various elements in LCO, LiFePO (LFP), and LiMn O (LMO) before
4 2 4
and after MC treatment in aqueous, acidic (Figure R6) and CO systems, aiming to
2
verify the raw material universality of the MC process.
The results in Figure R7 and R8 show that LCO exhibits a leaching trend similar
to that of ternary cathode materials. MC treatment increases the Li leaching efficiency
of LCO in the aqueous system from 0.52% to 43.51%, and in the acidic system, the Li
leaching efficiency reaches 91.71% with a Li selectivity of 91.9%, which are
significantly higher than the 21.98% Li leaching efficiency and 67.16% Li selectivity
of P-LCO. In contrast, LMO with a spinel structure shows a different leaching trend.
MC treatment does not lead to the formation of a large amount of soluble Li in LMO,
with the Li leaching efficiency in the aqueous system being only 14.93%. Although an
increasing trend in Li leaching efficiency and a decreasing trend in Mn leaching
efficiency are observed in the acidic system, the magnitude of the change is limited. P-
LMO already has a Li selectivity of 81.16% due to the stability of its framework, and
MC treatment only increases this value to 87.17%. LFP with an olivine structure has
better stability than layered materials; similar to LMO, MC treatment exerts a certain
effect on LFP but the effect is not significant. As shown in Figure R9, the MC process
can alleviate the challenge of weak acid (CO ) in leaching LCO and LMO, though its
2
effect is limited, increasing the Li leaching efficiency to slightly above 50%. In contrast,
for LFP, the MC treatment does not alter its leaching behavior under the weakly acidic
conditions provided by CO .
results shown in Figure R10. Both LCO and ternary materials exhibit a similar
amorphization trend during the MC process, but the degree of amorphization of MA-
LCO is lower, which is consistent with the result that less soluble Li is generated after
MC process. An increase in mechanical energy input might improve the efficiency of
the Li extraction process. For LMO, the XRD pattern only shows uniform broadening
and weakening of the diffraction peaks of all crystal planes, with no obvious structural
transformation similar to that of ternary cathode materials observed. Part of Li was
extracted though the MC-induced reduction of Mn4+ or Mn3+. The diffraction peaks of
the MA-LFP product also shows uniform weakening. Combined with earlier studies
(Green Chem., 2022, 24: 152-162; Mater. Today 2024, 73:130-150), it is known that
the selective Li extraction of LFP mostly needs to be achieved in the presence of
oxidants or an oxidizing atmosphere. However, the effect of mechanical energy on
NCM and LCO is similar to that of a reducing agent. Therefore, the current process
system may not be the optimal choice for Li extraction from LFP. In the future, if an
oxidizing atmosphere or oxidant is introduced during the MC process, more efficient
selective Li extraction from LFP may be achieved. The above supplementary results
indicate that the MC process has more significant applicability to layered materials
(ternary materials and LCO), while its effect on non-layered materials (LMO, LFP) is
limited due to structural and compositional differences, which provides a direction for
subsequent process optimization.

The authors detected oxygen vacancies in the leaching residue, while at which stage

Discussion:
Thank you for your perceptive question. In response to your inquiry, we have
supplemented the oxygen vacancy characterization results of products at various stages

at g = 2.003 were detected in all samples except for the leaching residue MA-NCM811-

NCM811, and the reasons for this are as follows. MA-NCM811 was prepared under
optimal activation conditions, where the original crystal structure of NCM811 was
significantly destroyed, and the valence states of local TM were reduced. However,
EPR results showed no obvious oxygen vacancies at this stage. It is suggested that
lattice oxygen may have been released in the form of O by losing electrons during the
2
activation process, without forming stable oxygen vacancies. Alternatively, some
crystal planes exposed during the MC process might have adsorbed inorganic functional
groups from the air, which could occupy oxygen vacancies (J. Power Sources, 2019,
432: 8-15). However, since MA-NCM811-WL also showed no obvious oxygen
vacancy signals, this possibility is ruled out.
In contrast, oxygen vacancies were generated in MA-NCM811-CO L. This
2
suggests that the extraction of lattice Li or TM remaining in the Li TMO framework
1-x 2-y

maintain charge neutrality, O2- are synchronously extracted, leading to the formation of
oxygen vacancies in the lattice (Chem. Eng. J., 2023, 463: 142316; Energy Storage
Mater., 2025, 79: 104307) and ultimately endowing the leaching residue MA-NCM811-
CO L with oxygen vacancy characteristics.

defined. Will the surface be easily peeling off if a reconstructed layer is formed?
Discussion:
Thank you for your insightful question. The surface reconstruction layer
mentioned in Section 2.3 of the manuscript was characterized primarily through TOF-
SIMS and XPS analysis of the activated product (Figure R12). We define the surface
reconstruction layer as a surface-modified zone, induced by mechanochemical
activation, characterized by distinct crystalline phase transitions and continuous depth-
dependent chemical gradients. Furthermore, this surface reconstruction layer
demonstrates significant stability against delamination. Because it forms a continuous
transitional structure to the underlying bulk phase, with a blurred boundary rather than
a sharp heterointerface with a fundamentally different composition or crystal structure.
Therefore, this continuous gradient inherent to the mechanochemically-induced
transformation distinguishes it sharply from discrete, deposited external coatings or
surface layers (e.g., via ALD or CVD) (Nanotechnol. Rev., 2017, 6 (6): 527-547; Adv.
Sci., 2016, 3 (10)), eliminating the weak interfaces typically susceptible to detachment.
Relevant revision has been added to Section 2.3. We appreciate your suggestion,
which helps to deepen the understanding of the relationship between the MC process
and leaching process.

Issue 2:
In addition to destroying the crystal structure, the MC process will also reduce the
particle size. Together with the size reduction, how it is related to the leaching process,
including lithium and other elements?
Discussion：
Thank you for your perceptive question. Our initial manuscript did not thoroughly
explore the relationship between these morphological alterations and the leaching
behavior. We will address this gap through supplementary experimental investigations.
Firstly, we explored the effect of the particle size on the leaching process by
experimental design. To specifically target our analysis, ethanol was introduced as
lubricant during MC process. The objective was to preferentially direct mechanical
energy towards particle size reduction rather than primary crystal structure destruction.
As shown in Figures R13 and R14, the introduction of ethanol cannot suppress
NCM811 particle fragmentation, while retain the integrity of the phase structure. The
leaching behaviors of the MC product with the assisting of ethanol (MA-NCM811-WE)
in aqueous and acidic systems was then evaluated to isolate the effects of mere particle
size reduction on Li and TMs leaching efficiencies. As shown in Figure R15, it
demonstrates that solely reducing particle size fails to alter the differential leaching
behavior between Li and TMs. Consequently, it cannot enable the preferential or
selective Li extraction under mild conditions.
In contrast, the MC route employed in this study was precisely optimized. At the
optimal activation conditions, it successfully induces targeted amorphization of the
NCM811 structure accompanied by a surface reconstruction layer forming Li-rich
domains as Figure R16. The effect of structural amorphization on the selective leaching
of Li is more important than the change of particle size.
The additional results and corresponding discussions have been incorporated into
Section 2.1 and Supplementary Note 2 (Determination of the key driving factors in
the MC process) of the revised manuscript. We thank the reviewer again for their
insightful comments, which have greatly strengthened our analysis of the MC process.

A detailed description on how the amorphous content in Figure 1 was determined
should be provided. How is the amorphous phase influencing the subsequent recycling
process?
Discussion:
Thank you for pointing out the issue. As shown in Figure 1b, the crystal structure
of LTMO undergoes an amorphization evolution during the MC process. To better
resolve this disordered structure, a combination of internal standard method and XRD
Rietveld refinement was employed to conduct an in-depth analysis of the amorphous
phase composition and crystalline structure of MA-NCM811 (J. Appl. Crystallogr.,
2001, 34 (2):196-202). The specific procedures are as follows. Si powder with 100%
crystallinity was used as the internal standard (with a mass proportion of 25%). XRD
data were collected using a Rigaku SmartLab 9 kW diffractometer (Cu Kα radiation,
scanning range 5°~90°, step size 0.01°, scanning speed 3°/min). The XRD patterns were
refined using Highscore5.3 software, and the Rietveld quantitative analysis without
standards was employed to calculate the relative contents of NCM811 and Si. The
content of Si was corrected to 25% to convert to absolute contents, and the proportion
of the amorphous phase in the mixture was calculated by 100%-crystalline phase
content-25%. The amorphous content in LTMO was further calculated by dividing the
amorphous content in the mixture by (1-25%). The related revision was supplemented
in Experimental section and Supplementary Note 1 (Determination of amorphous
phase fraction) of the revised manuscript.
The influence of the amorphous phase on subsequent recycling can be viewed
from two aspects. First, it promotes the highly efficient separation of Li and TMs in a
weakly acidic environment (provided by H O or CO ). Specifically, in an aqueous
2 2
system, approximately 75% of the Li can be effectively extracted without damaging the
crystalline structure of the activated product. This indicates that the extracted Li
originates mainly from the amorphous phase, which also accounts for the near-complete
Li extraction observed in the CO system. Second, the release of Li is not solely due to
2
the water-soluble nature of the Li-rich amorphous phase. A small portion results from
an exchange reaction between Li+ and H+. This process not only leaves behind a highly
disordered TM-based skeleton in the leaching product, but also introduces surface
hydroxyl groups, which offer potential advantages for subsequent applications in OER
catalysis.

The following are reviewer comments for the article entitled A Three-in-One
Strategy: Li/TMs Micro-Segregation to Enable Upcycling of Spent Layered Cathode
Materials submitted to Nature Communications by Wang et al. The reviewed article has
successfully demonstrated the novel approach of the selective Li recovery from spent
Li-ion cathodes and upgrading of transition metals during mechanochemical processes
assisted by CO2 sequestration. The Authors performed the broad compositional and
structural products analysis and OER catalytic activity. I recommend publishing the
article after a major review, and below are the comments and remarks:
Issue 1:
Could the Authors describe the XRD results shown in Figure 1b by ascribing the peaks
to the proper compounds?
Discussion:
Thank you for your thought-provoking question. As mentioned in lines 116-120
of Section 2.1, the MC process transforms the LTMO material from an R-3m layered
structure gradually into a disordered rock-salt phase with an Fm-3m space group.
However, we did not ascribe the XRD pattern of this activated product to any specific
compound for the following reasons.
First, the results in Figure 1b were collected from MA-NCM811 obtained by high-
energy ball milling of P-NCM811 under different activation time. Compared with the
P-NCM811, the diffraction peaks of MA-NCM811 exhibit an overall weakening and
broadening trend, with significant changes in certain characteristic peaks, particularly
the (003) peak, which shows a substantial reduction in intensity and nearly disappears.
These observations indicate that the MC process disrupts the long-range order of the
original crystal and drives its transition toward an amorphous state. Rietveld refinement
results further confirm that the amorphous phase has become the dominant component
of the MA product. Figure R1 clearly illustrates the gradual evolution from a crystalline

Discussion：
Thank you for your question. Regarding the changes in the morphology of
NCM811 during the MC process, we did not pay sufficient attention to this aspect in
our initial work. We now supplement the SEM results (Figure R23) before and after
MC treatment and related explanations. The original particles are regularly spherical
with a particle size of approximately 5-10 μm. After MC treatment, the particles
gradually break into nano-scale irregular fine particles. The specific trend of changes is
as follows: when activated for 1 h, there are still large particles that are not completely
destroyed; as the activation time is prolonged, the large particles disappear, but the
broken fine particles begin to aggregate gradually; when activated for 16 h, aggregates
with a particle size of 500 nm appear. This phenomenon is mainly attributed to the shear
force and extrusion effect generated by the impact of the ball milling medium, which
cause refinement of the particles. With the continuous input of mechanical energy, the
refined particles, due to their high surface energy, then re-aggregate. This result has
been consolidated into the Section 2.1, 2.3 and Supplementary Note 2
(Determination of the key driving factors in the MC process) of the revised
manuscript. We are grateful to the reviewer for the thorough critique, which has greatly
improved the integrity of our work.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents a short-range clean recycling approach for spent lithium-ion battery cathodes, convincingly demonstrating the efficiency of mechanochemical processes through robust evidence. The mechnochemical treatment enables recycling of spent NCM battery under relatively mild conditions. With carbonation of the as-treated black mass, lithium and transition metals recovery are both achieved. Nevertheless, there are still issues required to be discussed before publication.
In extracting valuable metals from spent cathode materials, CO2 as leaching reagent is usually considered as inefficient. The authors should provide detailed discussion on how the mechnochemical treatment enables a high reaction potential. Will the amorphous phase be important during the processing? How was the optimal activation time was determined?
- Improvement on discussion of state-of-the-art of literature is very necessary and how selective leaching and upcycling of cathode materials are explored should be added in the introduction section.
- The authors mentioned “Notably, prolonged activation time (activation time >2 h) leads to gradual dissolution of TMs”. What are gradual dissolution and how the dissolution the transition metals reacting with CO2? It is necessary to provide direct evidence on the intermediate products. Additionally, a thermodynamic analysis will be helpful for understanding the process.
- The research object of the manuscript focuses on ternary materials. Is LCO with a layered structure also feasible? Is LiFePO4 or LiMn2O4 also feasible? Can some experiments or explanations be added to improve the universality of the raw materials?
- The authors detected oxygen vacancies in the leaching residue, while at which stage the oxygen vacancies appeared is required to be clarified. For example, do oxygen vacancies exist in the mechanically activated products? Or do oxygen vacancies exist in the waste materials used in this study? Additional results is recommended to improve understanding the mechanisms.
- In Figure 3, the authors claims “a Li-rich surface reconstruction layer have been established on the surface of materials.” However, it is not clear how the layer is defined. Will the surface be easily peeling off if a reconstructed layer is formed?
- Error bars for the leaching efficiencies in the corresponding figures are required to be added to reflect the repeatability and statistical validity of the data.

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the authors proposed a three-in-one strategy that enables CO2-carbonation with spent cathode materials to achieve selective Li recovery and regeneration of transition metals. The study conducts an in-depth analysis of how mechnochemical (MC) treatment affects the reactivity of different elements in cathode materials and the underlying mechanisms, providing new insights on the role of MC treatment in the recycling process. I think it can be considered for publication if the following concerns are tackled with.
(1)The introduction can be enriched and a more detailed discussion on selective leaching and direct regeneration is required to be included. The authors only mentioned briefly the pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgical methods at this version and the statement on “...process requires a large amount of strong acid and alkali...” is not always correct. It is necessary to provide an outline on how this research is correlated and different from a traditional hydrometallurgical process.
(2)In addition to destroying the crystal structure, the MC process will also reduce the particle size. Together with the size reduction, how it is related to the leaching process, including lithium and other elements?
(3)A detailed description on how the amorphous content in Figure 1 was determined should be provided. How is the amorphous phase influencing the subsequent recycling process?
(4)What is the phase of the residual Li in the leaching product? It is required to discuss the carbonation process and how CO2 pressure and leaching time influence the lithium extraction.
(5)On page 10, the author present the Raman spectrum data of P-NCM811 and MA-NCM811 in Figure 4c. However, this section is unclearly articulated and lacks a robust connection to the contextual discussion. It is advised to revise this part for better coherence.
(6)Some details in Figures still need to be noted. In Figure 4e, the scale of TEM results is missing; in Figure 5e, the unit of the y-axis should be revised to mA cm-2.

### Reviewer 3

The following are reviewer comments for the article entitled A Three-in-One Strategy: Li/TMs Micro-Segregation to Enable Upcycling of Spent Layered Cathode Materials submitted to Nature Communications by Wang et al.
The reviewed article has successfully demonstrated the novel approach of the selective Li recovery from spent Li-ion cathodes and upgrading of transition metals during mechanochemical processes assisted by CO2 sequestration. The Authors performed the broad compositional and structural products analysis and OER catalytic activity. I recommend publishing the article after a major review, and below are the comments and remarks:
1. Could the Authors describe the XRD results shown in Figure 1b by ascribing the peaks to the proper compounds?
2. What purity do the recovered Li compounds exhibit?
3. How does the morphology (e.g., grain size, grain shape) of examined materials change upon mechanochemical processing? Whether SEM analysis was done before and after the MC process?
4. Were OER experiments performed also for benchmark OER materials e.g. RuO2 or Co3O4 for comparison with recovered catalyst materials?
5. At which potential were the chronoamperometry measurements performed shown in Fig. 5e?
6. 6. The description of the Y axis should be “current density” instead of “current”.
7. The Electrochemical Active Surface Area should be ascertained in order to assess the OER catalytic capabilities.

## Introduction

Consequently, the efficient recovery of critical metals from spent LIBs is crucial for economic, environmental,andsocialsustainability5,6.

Current recycling of critical metals from spent LIBs relies on threeprincipalroutes:pyrometallurgy,hydrometallurgy,anddirectregeneration7. indicate that the MC process has more significant applicability to layered materials
(ternary materials and LCO), while its effect on non-layered materials (LMO, LFP) is
limited due to structural and compositional differences, which provides a direction for
subsequent process optimization.

Discussion:
Thank you for your insightful question. The surface reconstruction layer
mentioned in Section 2.3 of the manuscript was characterized primarily through TOF-
SIMS and XPS analysis of the activated product (Figure R12). We define the surface
reconstruction layer as a surface-modified zone, induced by mechanochemical
activation, characterized by distinct crystalline phase transitions and continuous depth-
dependent chemical gradients. Furthermore, this surface reconstruction layer
demonstrates significant stability against delamination. Because it forms a continuous
transitional structure to the underlying bulk phase, with a blurred boundary rather than
a sharp heterointerface with a fundamentally different composition or crystal structure.
Therefore, this continuous gradient inherent to the mechanochemically-induced
transformation distinguishes it sharply from discrete, deposited external coatings or
surface layers (e.g., via ALD or CVD) (Nanotechnol. Rev., 2017, 6 (6): 527-547; Adv.
Sci., 2016, 3 (10)), eliminating the weak interfaces typically susceptible to detachment.

Issue 2:
In addition to destroying the crystal structure, the MC process will also reduce the
particle size. Together with the size reduction, how it is related to the leaching process,
including lithium and other elements?
Discussion：
Thank you for your perceptive question. Our initial manuscript did not thoroughly
explore the relationship between these morphological alterations and the leaching
behavior. We will address this gap through supplementary experimental investigations.
Firstly, we explored the effect of the particle size on the leaching process by
experimental design. To specifically target our analysis, ethanol was introduced as
lubricant during MC process. The objective was to preferentially direct mechanical
energy towards particle size reduction rather than primary crystal structure destruction.
As shown in Figures R13 and R14, the introduction of ethanol cannot suppress
NCM811 particle fragmentation, while retain the integrity of the phase structure. The
leaching behaviors of the MC product with the assisting of ethanol (MA-NCM811-WE)
in aqueous and acidic systems was then evaluated to isolate the effects of mere particle
size reduction on Li and TMs leaching efficiencies. As shown in Figure R15, it
demonstrates that solely reducing particle size fails to alter the differential leaching
behavior between Li and TMs. Consequently, it cannot enable the preferential or
selective Li extraction under mild conditions.
In contrast, the MC route employed in this study was precisely optimized. At the
optimal activation conditions, it successfully induces targeted amorphization of the
NCM811 structure accompanied by a surface reconstruction layer forming Li-rich
domains as Figure R16. The effect of structural amorphization on the selective leaching
of Li is more important than the change of particle size.
The additional results and corresponding discussions have been incorporated into
Section 2.1 and Supplementary Note 2 (Determination of the key driving factors in
the MC process) of the revised manuscript. We thank the reviewer again for their
insightful comments, which have greatly strengthened our analysis of the MC process.

A detailed description on how the amorphous content in Figure 1 was determined
should be provided. How is the amorphous phase influencing the subsequent recycling
process?
Discussion:
Thank you for pointing out the issue. As shown in Figure 1b, the crystal structure
of LTMO undergoes an amorphization evolution during the MC process. To better
resolve this disordered structure, a combination of internal standard method and XRD
Rietveld refinement was employed to conduct an in-depth analysis of the amorphous
phase composition and crystalline structure of MA-NCM811 (J. Appl. Crystallogr.,
2001, 34 (2):196-202). The specific procedures are as follows. Si powder with 100%
crystallinity was used as the internal standard (with a mass proportion of 25%). XRD
data were collected using a Rigaku SmartLab 9 kW diffractometer (Cu Kα radiation,
scanning range 5°~90°, step size 0.01°, scanning speed 3°/min). The XRD patterns were
refined using Highscore5.3 software, and the Rietveld quantitative analysis without
standards was employed to calculate the relative contents of NCM811 and Si. The
content of Si was corrected to 25% to convert to absolute contents, and the proportion
of the amorphous phase in the mixture was calculated by 100%-crystalline phase
content-25%. The amorphous content in LTMO was further calculated by dividing the
amorphous content in the mixture by (1-25%). The related revision was supplemented
in Experimental section and Supplementary Note 1 (Determination of amorphous
phase fraction) of the revised manuscript.
The influence of the amorphous phase on subsequent recycling can be viewed
from two aspects. First, it promotes the highly efficient separation of Li and TMs in a
weakly acidic environment (provided by H O or CO ). Specifically, in an aqueous
2 2
system, approximately 75% of the Li can be effectively extracted without damaging the
crystalline structure of the activated product. This indicates that the extracted Li
originates mainly from the amorphous phase, which also accounts for the near-complete
Li extraction observed in the CO system. Second, the release of Li is not solely due to
2
the water-soluble nature of the Li-rich amorphous phase. A small portion results from
an exchange reaction between Li+ and H+. This process not only leaves behind a highly
disordered TM-based skeleton in the leaching product, but also introduces surface
hydroxyl groups, which offer potential advantages for subsequent applications in OER
catalysis.

The following are reviewer comments for the article entitled A Three-in-One
Strategy: Li/TMs Micro-Segregation to Enable Upcycling of Spent Layered Cathode
Materials submitted to Nature Communications by Wang et al. The reviewed article has
successfully demonstrated the novel approach of the selective Li recovery from spent
Li-ion cathodes and upgrading of transition metals during mechanochemical processes
assisted by CO2 sequestration. The Authors performed the broad compositional and
structural products analysis and OER catalytic activity. I recommend publishing the
article after a major review, and below are the comments and remarks:
Issue 1:
Could the Authors describe the XRD results shown in Figure 1b by ascribing the peaks
to the proper compounds?
Discussion:
Thank you for your thought-provoking question. As mentioned in lines 116-120
of Section 2.1, the MC process transforms the LTMO material from an R-3m layered
structure gradually into a disordered rock-salt phase with an Fm-3m space group.
However, we did not ascribe the XRD pattern of this activated product to any specific
compound for the following reasons.
First, the results in Figure 1b were collected from MA-NCM811 obtained by high-
energy ball milling of P-NCM811 under different activation time. Compared with the
P-NCM811, the diffraction peaks of MA-NCM811 exhibit an overall weakening and
broadening trend, with significant changes in certain characteristic peaks, particularly
the (003) peak, which shows a substantial reduction in intensity and nearly disappears.
These observations indicate that the MC process disrupts the long-range order of the
original crystal and drives its transition toward an amorphous state. Rietveld refinement
results further confirm that the amorphous phase has become the dominant component
of the MA product. Figure R1 clearly illustrates the gradual evolution from a crystalline
to an amorphous state, in which the residual crystalline regions also exhibit highly
disordered characteristics. It should be noted that, while we can deduce the general
amorphization pathway, the specific composition of the amorphous phase and the exact
nature of the residual crystalline phase remain unclear. Directly attributing the residual
characteristic peaks (their positions are close to those of TM oxides (TMOs) with rock-
salt structures, such as NiO) to a specific compound would contradict the mechanistic
understanding that high-energy ball milling in this system primarily induces physical
amorphization rather than the formation of new crystalline phases, and could mislead
subsequent research. Therefore, we interpret the residual peaks in Figure R1 as
diffraction signals originating from locally ordered regions that have undergone severe
mechanical damage but still retain the distorted structural features of NCM811. If the
reviewer has any valuable comments on this point, we look forward to further
discussion and clarification.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents a short-range clean recycling approach for spent lithium-ion battery cathodes, convincingly demonstrating the efficiency of mechanochemical processes through robust evidence. The mechnochemical treatment enables recycling of spent NCM battery under relatively mild conditions. With carbonation of the as-treated black mass, lithium and transition metals recovery are both achieved. Nevertheless, there are still issues required to be discussed before publication.
In extracting valuable metals from spent cathode materials, CO2 as leaching reagent is usually considered as inefficient. The authors should provide detailed discussion on how the mechnochemical treatment enables a high reaction potential. Will the amorphous phase be important during the processing? How was the optimal activation time was determined?
- Improvement on discussion of state-of-the-art of literature is very necessary and how selective leaching and upcycling of cathode materials are explored should be added in the introduction section.
- The authors mentioned “Notably, prolonged activation time (activation time >2 h) leads to gradual dissolution of TMs”. What are gradual dissolution and how the dissolution the transition metals reacting with CO2? It is necessary to provide direct evidence on the intermediate products. Additionally, a thermodynamic analysis will be helpful for understanding the process.
- The research object of the manuscript focuses on ternary materials. Is LCO with a layered structure also feasible? Is LiFePO4 or LiMn2O4 also feasible? Can some experiments or explanations be added to improve the universality of the raw materials?
- The authors detected oxygen vacancies in the leaching residue, while at which stage the oxygen vacancies appeared is required to be clarified. For example, do oxygen vacancies exist in the mechanically activated products? Or do oxygen vacancies exist in the waste materials used in this study? Additional results is recommended to improve understanding the mechanisms.
- In Figure 3, the authors claims “a Li-rich surface reconstruction layer have been established on the surface of materials.” However, it is not clear how the layer is defined. Will the surface be easily peeling off if a reconstructed layer is formed?
- Error bars for the leaching efficiencies in the corresponding figures are required to be added to reflect the repeatability and statistical validity of the data.

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the authors proposed a three-in-one strategy that enables CO2-carbonation with spent cathode materials to achieve selective Li recovery and regeneration of transition metals. The study conducts an in-depth analysis of how mechnochemical (MC) treatment affects the reactivity of different elements in cathode materials and the underlying mechanisms, providing new insights on the role of MC treatment in the recycling process. I think it can be considered for publication if the following concerns are tackled with.
(1)The introduction can be enriched and a more detailed discussion on selective leaching and direct regeneration is required to be included. The authors only mentioned briefly the pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgical methods at this version and the statement on “...process requires a large amount of strong acid and alkali...” is not always correct. It is necessary to provide an outline on how this research is correlated and different from a traditional hydrometallurgical process.
(2)In addition to destroying the crystal structure, the MC process will also reduce the particle size. Together with the size reduction, how it is related to the leaching process, including lithium and other elements?
(3)A detailed description on how the amorphous content in Figure 1 was determined should be provided. How is the amorphous phase influencing the subsequent recycling process?
(4)What is the phase of the residual Li in the leaching product? It is required to discuss the carbonation process and how CO2 pressure and leaching time influence the lithium extraction.
(5)On page 10, the author present the Raman spectrum data of P-NCM811 and MA-NCM811 in Figure 4c. However, this section is unclearly articulated and lacks a robust connection to the contextual discussion. It is advised to revise this part for better coherence.
(6)Some details in Figures still need to be noted. In Figure 4e, the scale of TEM results is missing; in Figure 5e, the unit of the y-axis should be revised to mA cm-2.

evidence, concluding structural evolution of LTMO and leaching performance of Li and

crystalline components. Second, the leaching results in Figure R2 indicate that the
activated product with activation time of 2h achieves a Li extraction yield of 75 % in
aqueous system, with no further significant improvement upon prolonged activation.
The effect is even more pronounced in the acidic system, 2 h of MC process gives the
highest Li leaching efficiency and selectivity, whereas longer activation times only
marginally increase Li recovery while substantially enhancing TMs dissolution. These
findings suggest that excessive activation triggers detrimental side reactions and
reduces Li selectivity. Therefore, 2 h is chosen as the optimal activation time, balancing
maximum structural disorder with the best Li recovery while avoiding the loss of
selectivity. Although this optimal condition was established for NCM811, it also proves
effective for other layered ternary cathodes such as NCM111 and NCM622.
Nonetheless, given the distinct structural characteristics of low-nickel ternary cathode
materials, further optimization of activation parameters is warranted and will be
explored in future work.

uniquely induces structural transformations in spent cathodes which could convert

Thank you very much for your insightful questions.
Regarding the mechanism of “gradual dissolution” of TM in the acidic system,
this study specifies that the phenomenon refers to the dynamic process whereby TM2+

phase and remain stable. As shown in Section 2.1, the leaching efficiencies of TMs
from MA-NCM811 initially decreases and then increases with prolonged activation
time, which stems from the modulating effect of mechanical activation duration on the
crystal structure. At the optimal activation time of 2 h, Li+ is sufficiently released while
TM ions remain well retained within a relatively intact lattice framework. And further
extending the activation time, TMs started to migrate into the solution. As for the reason
of TMs dissolution, we monitored the final pH in both aqueous and acidic systems

water-soluble Li+ reached saturation at 2 h. In contrast, the pH in the acidic system first

efficiency and an increase in TM leaching efficiencies, confirming that the leaching
pathways of Li and TMs evolve with mechanical energy input. Ultimately, excessive
activation time diminished the difference in leaching activity between Li and TM,

(e.g., Ni2+). We added the E-pH diagram (Figures R3b-d) obtained from HSC

Issue 4:
The research object of the manuscript focuses on ternary materials. Is LCO with a
layered structure also feasible? Is LiFePO4 or LiMn2O4 also feasible? Can some
experiments or explanations be added to improve the universality of the raw materials?
Discussion:
Thank you for your practical questions. This study initially focused primarily on
ternary materials with a layered structure. Owing to their unique structural
characteristics and Ni-containing content, the effect of mechanical energy is more
pronounced. However, we did neglect to investigate the impact of the MC process on
LiCoO (LCO) also with a layered structure, and other common non-layered cathode
2
materials. In response to your inquiry, we have supplemented the data on the leaching
efficiency of various elements in LCO, LiFePO (LFP), and LiMn O (LMO) before
4 2 4
and after MC treatment in aqueous, acidic (Figure R6) and CO systems, aiming to
2
verify the raw material universality of the MC process.
The results in Figure R7 and R8 show that LCO exhibits a leaching trend similar
to that of ternary cathode materials. MC treatment increases the Li leaching efficiency
of LCO in the aqueous system from 0.52% to 43.51%, and in the acidic system, the Li
leaching efficiency reaches 91.71% with a Li selectivity of 91.9%, which are
significantly higher than the 21.98% Li leaching efficiency and 67.16% Li selectivity
of P-LCO. In contrast, LMO with a spinel structure shows a different leaching trend.
MC treatment does not lead to the formation of a large amount of soluble Li in LMO,
with the Li leaching efficiency in the aqueous system being only 14.93%. Although an
increasing trend in Li leaching efficiency and a decreasing trend in Mn leaching
efficiency are observed in the acidic system, the magnitude of the change is limited. P-
LMO already has a Li selectivity of 81.16% due to the stability of its framework, and
MC treatment only increases this value to 87.17%. LFP with an olivine structure has
better stability than layered materials; similar to LMO, MC treatment exerts a certain
effect on LFP but the effect is not significant. As shown in Figure R9, the MC process
can alleviate the challenge of weak acid (CO ) in leaching LCO and LMO, though its
2
effect is limited, increasing the Li leaching efficiency to slightly above 50%. In contrast,
for LFP, the MC treatment does not alter its leaching behavior under the weakly acidic
conditions provided by CO .
results shown in Figure R10. Both LCO and ternary materials exhibit a similar
amorphization trend during the MC process, but the degree of amorphization of MA-
LCO is lower, which is consistent with the result that less soluble Li is generated after
MC process. An increase in mechanical energy input might improve the efficiency of
the Li extraction process. For LMO, the XRD pattern only shows uniform broadening
and weakening of the diffraction peaks of all crystal planes, with no obvious structural
transformation similar to that of ternary cathode materials observed. Part of Li was
extracted though the MC-induced reduction of Mn4+ or Mn3+. The diffraction peaks of
the MA-LFP product also shows uniform weakening. Combined with earlier studies
(Green Chem., 2022, 24: 152-162; Mater. Today 2024, 73:130-150), it is known that
the selective Li extraction of LFP mostly needs to be achieved in the presence of
oxidants or an oxidizing atmosphere. However, the effect of mechanical energy on
NCM and LCO is similar to that of a reducing agent. Therefore, the current process
system may not be the optimal choice for Li extraction from LFP. In the future, if an
oxidizing atmosphere or oxidant is introduced during the MC process, more efficient
selective Li extraction from LFP may be achieved. The above supplementary results
indicate that the MC process has more significant applicability to layered materials
(ternary materials and LCO), while its effect on non-layered materials (LMO, LFP) is
limited due to structural and compositional differences, which provides a direction for
subsequent process optimization.

Issue 5:
The authors detected oxygen vacancies in the leaching residue, while at which stage
the oxygen vacancies appeared is required to be clarified. For example, do oxygen
vacancies exist in the mechanically activated products? Or do oxygen vacancies exist
in the waste materials used in this study? Additional results is recommended to improve
understanding the mechanisms.
Discussion:
Thank you for your perceptive question. In response to your inquiry, we have
supplemented the oxygen vacancy characterization results of products at various stages
in the research route, as shown in Figure R11. It can be observed that no obvious signals
at g = 2.003 were detected in all samples except for the leaching residue MA-NCM811-
CO L obtained in the CO system. This indicates that oxygen vacancies do not appear
2 2
during the MC process but are generated during the leaching process in the CO system.
mechanical energy input, which theoretically affects the coordination environment of
elements within the lattice. However, no oxygen vacancies are generated in MA-
NCM811, and the reasons for this are as follows. MA-NCM811 was prepared under
optimal activation conditions, where the original crystal structure of NCM811 was
significantly destroyed, and the valence states of local TM were reduced. However,
EPR results showed no obvious oxygen vacancies at this stage. It is suggested that
lattice oxygen may have been released in the form of O by losing electrons during the
2
activation process, without forming stable oxygen vacancies. Alternatively, some
crystal planes exposed during the MC process might have adsorbed inorganic functional
groups from the air, which could occupy oxygen vacancies (J. Power Sources, 2019,
432: 8-15). However, since MA-NCM811-WL also showed no obvious oxygen
vacancy signals, this possibility is ruled out.
In contrast, oxygen vacancies were generated in MA-NCM811-CO L. This
2
suggests that the extraction of lattice Li or TM remaining in the Li TMO framework
1-x 2-y
disrupts the charge balance and coordination environment of the original lattice. To
maintain charge neutrality, O2- are synchronously extracted, leading to the formation of
oxygen vacancies in the lattice (Chem. Eng. J., 2023, 463: 142316; Energy Storage
Mater., 2025, 79: 104307) and ultimately endowing the leaching residue MA-NCM811-
CO L with oxygen vacancy characteristics.

Discussion:
Thank you for your insightful question. The surface reconstruction layer
mentioned in Section 2.3 of the manuscript was characterized primarily through TOF-
SIMS and XPS analysis of the activated product (Figure R12). We define the surface
reconstruction layer as a surface-modified zone, induced by mechanochemical
activation, characterized by distinct crystalline phase transitions and continuous depth-
dependent chemical gradients. Furthermore, this surface reconstruction layer
demonstrates significant stability against delamination. Because it forms a continuous
transitional structure to the underlying bulk phase, with a blurred boundary rather than
a sharp heterointerface with a fundamentally different composition or crystal structure.
Therefore, this continuous gradient inherent to the mechanochemically-induced
transformation distinguishes it sharply from discrete, deposited external coatings or
surface layers (e.g., via ALD or CVD) (Nanotechnol. Rev., 2017, 6 (6): 527-547; Adv.
Sci., 2016, 3 (10)), eliminating the weak interfaces typically susceptible to detachment.
Relevant revision has been added to Section 2.3. We appreciate your suggestion,
which helps to deepen the understanding of the relationship between the MC process
and leaching process.

Issue 2:
In addition to destroying the crystal structure, the MC process will also reduce the
particle size. Together with the size reduction, how it is related to the leaching process,
including lithium and other elements?
Discussion：
Thank you for your perceptive question. Our initial manuscript did not thoroughly
explore the relationship between these morphological alterations and the leaching
behavior. We will address this gap through supplementary experimental investigations.
Firstly, we explored the effect of the particle size on the leaching process by
experimental design. To specifically target our analysis, ethanol was introduced as
lubricant during MC process. The objective was to preferentially direct mechanical
energy towards particle size reduction rather than primary crystal structure destruction.
As shown in Figures R13 and R14, the introduction of ethanol cannot suppress
NCM811 particle fragmentation, while retain the integrity of the phase structure. The
leaching behaviors of the MC product with the assisting of ethanol (MA-NCM811-WE)
in aqueous and acidic systems was then evaluated to isolate the effects of mere particle
size reduction on Li and TMs leaching efficiencies. As shown in Figure R15, it
demonstrates that solely reducing particle size fails to alter the differential leaching
behavior between Li and TMs. Consequently, it cannot enable the preferential or
selective Li extraction under mild conditions.
In contrast, the MC route employed in this study was precisely optimized. At the
optimal activation conditions, it successfully induces targeted amorphization of the
NCM811 structure accompanied by a surface reconstruction layer forming Li-rich
domains as Figure R16. The effect of structural amorphization on the selective leaching
of Li is more important than the change of particle size.
The additional results and corresponding discussions have been incorporated into
Section 2.1 and Supplementary Note 2 (Determination of the key driving factors in
the MC process) of the revised manuscript. We thank the reviewer again for their
insightful comments, which have greatly strengthened our analysis of the MC process.

phase composition and crystalline structure of MA-NCM811 (J. Appl. Crystallogr.,
2001, 34 (2):196-202). The specific procedures are as follows. Si powder with 100%
crystallinity was used as the internal standard (with a mass proportion of 25%). XRD
data were collected using a Rigaku SmartLab 9 kW diffractometer (Cu Kα radiation,
scanning range 5°~90°, step size 0.01°, scanning speed 3°/min). The XRD patterns were
refined using Highscore5.3 software, and the Rietveld quantitative analysis without
standards was employed to calculate the relative contents of NCM811 and Si. The
content of Si was corrected to 25% to convert to absolute contents, and the proportion
of the amorphous phase in the mixture was calculated by 100%-crystalline phase
content-25%. The amorphous content in LTMO was further calculated by dividing the
amorphous content in the mixture by (1-25%). The related revision was supplemented
in Experimental section and Supplementary Note 1 (Determination of amorphous
phase fraction) of the revised manuscript.
The influence of the amorphous phase on subsequent recycling can be viewed
from two aspects. First, it promotes the highly efficient separation of Li and TMs in a
weakly acidic environment (provided by H O or CO ). Specifically, in an aqueous
2 2
system, approximately 75% of the Li can be effectively extracted without damaging the
crystalline structure of the activated product. This indicates that the extracted Li
originates mainly from the amorphous phase, which also accounts for the near-complete
Li extraction observed in the CO system. Second, the release of Li is not solely due to
2
the water-soluble nature of the Li-rich amorphous phase. A small portion results from
an exchange reaction between Li+ and H+. This process not only leaves behind a highly
disordered TM-based skeleton in the leaching product, but also introduces surface
hydroxyl groups, which offer potential advantages for subsequent applications in OER
catalysis.

The following are reviewer comments for the article entitled A Three-in-One
Strategy: Li/TMs Micro-Segregation to Enable Upcycling of Spent Layered Cathode
Materials submitted to Nature Communications by Wang et al. The reviewed article has
successfully demonstrated the novel approach of the selective Li recovery from spent
Li-ion cathodes and upgrading of transition metals during mechanochemical processes
assisted by CO2 sequestration. The Authors performed the broad compositional and
structural products analysis and OER catalytic activity. I recommend publishing the
article after a major review, and below are the comments and remarks:
Issue 1:
Could the Authors describe the XRD results shown in Figure 1b by ascribing the peaks
to the proper compounds?
Discussion:
Thank you for your thought-provoking question. As mentioned in lines 116-120
of Section 2.1, the MC process transforms the LTMO material from an R-3m layered
structure gradually into a disordered rock-salt phase with an Fm-3m space group.
However, we did not ascribe the XRD pattern of this activated product to any specific
compound for the following reasons.
First, the results in Figure 1b were collected from MA-NCM811 obtained by high-
energy ball milling of P-NCM811 under different activation time. Compared with the
P-NCM811, the diffraction peaks of MA-NCM811 exhibit an overall weakening and
broadening trend, with significant changes in certain characteristic peaks, particularly
the (003) peak, which shows a substantial reduction in intensity and nearly disappears.
These observations indicate that the MC process disrupts the long-range order of the
original crystal and drives its transition toward an amorphous state. Rietveld refinement
results further confirm that the amorphous phase has become the dominant component
of the MA product. Figure R1 clearly illustrates the gradual evolution from a crystalline
to an amorphous state, in which the residual crystalline regions also exhibit highly
disordered characteristics. It should be noted that, while we can deduce the general
amorphization pathway, the specific composition of the amorphous phase and the exact
nature of the residual crystalline phase remain unclear. Directly attributing the residual
characteristic peaks (their positions are close to those of TM oxides (TMOs) with rock-
salt structures, such as NiO) to a specific compound would contradict the mechanistic
understanding that high-energy ball milling in this system primarily induces physical
amorphization rather than the formation of new crystalline phases, and could mislead
subsequent research. Therefore, we interpret the residual peaks in Figure R1 as
diffraction signals originating from locally ordered regions that have undergone severe
mechanical damage but still retain the distorted structural features of NCM811. If the
reviewer has any valuable comments on this point, we look forward to further
discussion and clarification.

Issue 3:
How does the morphology (e.g., grain size, grain shape) of examined materials change
upon mechanochemical processing? Whether SEM analysis was done before and after
the MC process?
Discussion：
Thank you for your question. Regarding the changes in the morphology of
NCM811 during the MC process, we did not pay sufficient attention to this aspect in
our initial work. We now supplement the SEM results (Figure R23) before and after
MC treatment and related explanations. The original particles are regularly spherical
with a particle size of approximately 5-10 μm. After MC treatment, the particles
gradually break into nano-scale irregular fine particles. The specific trend of changes is
as follows: when activated for 1 h, there are still large particles that are not completely
destroyed; as the activation time is prolonged, the large particles disappear, but the
broken fine particles begin to aggregate gradually; when activated for 16 h, aggregates
with a particle size of 500 nm appear. This phenomenon is mainly attributed to the shear
force and extrusion effect generated by the impact of the ball milling medium, which
cause refinement of the particles. With the continuous input of mechanical energy, the
refined particles, due to their high surface energy, then re-aggregate. This result has
been consolidated into the Section 2.1, 2.3 and Supplementary Note 2
(Determination of the key driving factors in the MC process) of the revised
manuscript. We are grateful to the reviewer for the thorough critique, which has greatly
improved the integrity of our work.
